question: A manager takes one Claude-drafted announcement about a service change and, in three separate conversations, has it reworked for staff, for customers and for the regulator. She sends all three without ever reading them side by side. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) The three versions adopt slightly different tones of voice, so the organisation sounds less consistent than its style guide requires.
B) The three versions end up at noticeably different lengths, so some audiences receive a considerably fuller account of the change than others.
C) The three versions drift apart on the substance, so different audiences are told different things and an outsider finds the discrepancy.
D) The three conversations consume more of her weekly allowance than adapting the announcement once inside a single conversation would.
correct_answers: C) The three versions drift apart on the substance, so different audiences are told different things and an outsider finds the discrepancy.
explanations: Tone variation between audiences is largely intended, and an inconsistent voice is a presentational problem. It is a much smaller concern than the underlying facts differing between the three versions.

Different lengths for different audiences are usually appropriate rather than a defect; a regulator and a customer legitimately need different amounts of detail. Length alone does not create a contradiction.

Correct. Adapting independently lets the facts, dates and commitments diverge, and because nobody compared the versions the inconsistency surfaces externally, in the worst case in front of the regulator.

Three conversations use somewhat more allowance than one, but that is a modest efficiency cost. It is far outweighed by the possibility of telling a regulator something different from what customers were told.
